Pyxel repository distributed a credential-stealing workflow

Target: Pyxel · repo
Date: 2026-10-08
Target Kind: project
Language: Shell
Cause: compromised_account_credentials
Impact: credential_theft
Phase: source

Synopsis

A compromised contributor account added a malicious GitHub Actions workflow to Pyxel. The workflow attempted to send repository credentials to an attacker-controlled server.

Story

A purported security audit in Pyxel's repository was designed to hand the project's publishing credentials to an outsider. The October 8 intrusion used the account of Takashi Kitao, the maintainer of the Python retro-game engine, to add and revise a GitHub Actions workflow. StepSecurity documented three malicious commits and two additional manual executions during the attacker's activity.

Pyxel helped developers make games with deliberately small palettes and simple sound capabilities, but its release machinery held credentials with much broader consequences. In the retained security-audit.yml, the attacker's command explicitly referenced CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN, PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN, PYPI_PASSWORD, and PYPI_USERNAME. These were the names of secrets the workflow asked GitHub to supply, not credentials hardcoded in the sample. Their values, if available to the job, were assembled for transmission to an external IP address.

The workflow also requested a full checkout and scanned both current files and Git history for cloud, source-control, and AI-service credential patterns. Static inspection showed that it collected nearby lines around AWS key identifiers, allowing associated secrets to accompany a match. Historical scanning was bounded by command-output limits, and matching a credential-shaped string did not prove it was still usable. Deleting a secret from the latest source file would not remove it from the history the workflow searched.

OpenSourceMalware placed Pyxel in the renewed GhostAction account-compromise campaign. StepSecurity recorded five successful workflow runs, but those status results did not reveal the exact credentials stolen. The public evidence established malicious automation in the upstream repository and access to its execution path; it did not establish a malicious PyPI or crates.io release of Pyxel. A workflow removal alone could not demonstrate that any credentials already transmitted had been invalidated.
